newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. urges action to discourage Israeli settlements.
newsitem.headline: U.N. urges action to discourage Israeli settlements.

text.p: The General Assembly recommended on Tuesday that U.N. members "actively discourage" activities that contribute to Israeli settlement-building in occupied territories, and demanded that Israel provide information about goods produced in the settlements.
The vote on the resolution, at a resumed emergency special session of the Assembly, was 131 to three with 14 abstentions.

Voting against were Israel, Micronesia and the United States. Abstaining were: Andorra, Australia, Costa Rica, Croatia, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Marshall Islands, Nicaragua, Romania, Russia, Rwanda, Slovakia and Uzbekistan.

The draft was based on an earlier version that was softened to attract maximum support, including that of all 15 European Union members except Germany. Russia, co-sponsor with the United States of the Middle East peace process, abstained.

The resolution condemns Israel's failure to comply with a resolution adopted in April by 134 votes to three -- again Israel, Micronesia and the United States -- with 11 abstentions, demanding that it cease construction of 6,500 homes at a site south of Jerusalem captured in the 1967 Middle East war called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.
A recent report by Secretary-General Kofi Annan criticising Israel's continued building prompted Arab U.N. members to call for a resumption of the special session.

The new resolution recommends that the parties to the Fourth Geneva Convention, which bars settlements in occupied territory, convene a conference on measures to enforce the convention and asks the U.N. secretary-general to provide a report in three months.

In a move toward sanctions, which only the Security Council can make binding, the resolution recommends that U.N. members "actively discourage activities which directly contribute to any construction or development of Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory, including Jerusalem."
It demands that Israel "make available to member states the necessary information about goods produced or manufactured in the illegal settlements" -- presumably so they can be boycotted.

A tougher earlier version would have specifically requested that U.N. members halt any support by companies and individuals for Israeli settlements and to bar the import of any goods produced or made in the settlements.

An earlier version would also have moved toward barring Israel from the 185-member U.N. body, stressing that "normal participation...in the workings of the General Assembly cannot be carried out" while a state is violating international law and U.N. resolutions.

This was replaced with language from the U.N. Charter stressing that members, "in order to ensure their rights and benefits from membership, should fulfil in good faith the obligations assumed by them" in accordance with the Charter.
Speaking before the vote, United States U.N. envoy Bill Richardson called the draft "a partisan resolution aimed not at building confidence or dialogue but at confrontation."
"The specifics of this resolution will not serve the cause of peace in the Middle East," he added, while reiterating U.S. opposition to construction at Har Homa.

Richardson, whose country is the main sponsor of Mideast negotiations, said the demand for a "partial economic boycott of Israel" ran counter to a basic building block of the peace process. He also criticised language, "explicit or implicit, threatening the participation of any member state in the General Assembly" and opposed a conference of the parties to the Fourth Geneva Convention.
The Assembly was again adjourned only temporarily, making another resumption likely, possibly after the secretary-general's next report in mid-October.
